name: Cica / Centella asiatica
lead: Cica is the skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, a perennial herb also called gotu kola, Asiatic pennywort or Indian pennywort. Its extracts and isolated triterpenoids (asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid) go into soothing creams, serums, masks and ampoules that people use to calm irritated, reddened skin and to support recovery after blemishes, wounds and scarring, leaving a smoother, calmer-looking complexion [1][2].

Reviews describe laboratory and clinical work in which the plant's triterpenes promote fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis and improve the strength of newly formed skin, and they discuss its use in small wounds, hypertrophic scars, burns, photoaging, cellulite and stretch marks [2][3][5][6]. Wikipedia reports traditional use for skin conditions and minor wounds, while noting that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research [1]. Recent randomised studies of moisturisers containing the extract report improvements in rosacea-related redness, bruise appearance and crepey skin, and a trial of an oral extract reported reductions in wrinkle depth [13].

In routines, cica usually plays a supporting role: a soothing layer used alongside moisturisers and sunscreen, particularly after breakouts, over-exfoliation or procedures. The plant is also eaten as a leafy green across Asia and taken as an herbal supplement [1]. The product term 'Cica' is also the brand name of a silicone gel sheeting for scars that is unrelated to the herb [8].

paras: Cica products are applied topically to soothe sensitive or irritated skin and to support recovery after blemishes, scrapes and scarring, with the visible aim of less redness and more even-looking skin [1][2]. A review of Centella asiatica in cosmetology says the extract has been examined for photoaging skin, cellulite and stretch marks, with a mechanism involving increased collagen synthesis and fibronectin content [3].

Formulations range from creams, gels and sheet masks containing plant extract to products built around purified madecassoside or asiaticoside. Recent studies have tested the extract paired with other ingredients such as mandelic acid, ceramide and panthenol in moisturisers [13].

The plant has been used for centuries in folk medicine and is described in one review as a 'panacea' about 3,000 years ago [2]. Reviews report ethnomedicinal use in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine, including for memory and brain function; asiaticoside and madecassoside are the marker compounds named in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia [4].

Centella asiatica is a slender, creeping herbaceous perennial with long-stalked, rounded green leaves and tiny white or crimson flowers, native to tropical Africa, Asia, Australia and western Pacific islands. It grows in swampy areas, matures in about three months and is harvested by hand [1]. Its common names include gotu kola, Indian pennywort, spadeleaf and coinwort [1].

About 124 compounds have been identified, chiefly pentacyclic triterpenoids and their glycosides; named constituents include asiatic acid, madecassic acid, asiaticoside and madecassoside [1]. Individual plants can be diploid, tetraploid or hexaploid, and a chromosome-level genome published in 2021 helps explain how the plant produces its triterpenoids; a telomere-to-telomere genome followed in 2025 [1]. Because the plant is aquatic it can absorb pollutants, has been studied as a phytoextraction plant for heavy metals, and is considered highly invasive on several Pacific islands [1].

Centella is a food plant in many cuisines. In Burma the raw leaves form the base of a salad with onion, peanuts and a lime and fish-sauce dressing; in Sri Lanka the leafy green called malluma is eaten with rice and curries and made into a porridge called kola kanda; in Indonesia and Malaysia it appears in salads and ulam; in Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam it is made into drinks or added to rolls; and in Bangladesh and West Bengal it is used in fritters [1].

Names vary widely: gotu kola and vallaarai in Sri Lanka and India, pegaga in Malay and Indonesian, bai bua bok in Thai, jixuecao in Chinese, tsubokusa in Japanese, byeongpul in Korean, rau ma in Vietnamese and mandukaparni in Hindi [1].

Laboratory and animal work described in reviews reports promotion of fibroblast proliferation, increased collagen and fibronectin synthesis, better tensile strength of newly formed skin, and dampening of the inflammatory phase in hypertrophic scars and keloids [2][3]. Reviews of asiaticoside and madecassoside list anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, wound-healing and anti-ageing activities among their reported properties across studies from 2005 to 2022 [4]. A 2023 review of asiatic acid describes extracts as promoting fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis [6][14].

A 2024 review of topical use in wound care reports that the four main compounds support collagen synthesis, reduce inflammation and provide antioxidant effects, and that delivery systems such as hydrogels, nanostructures and microneedles are being studied for faster healing [5][14].

Reviews of the topical literature summarise experimental and clinical work on wound healing, hypertrophic scars and burns [2][5][6]. A 2013 cosmetology review reports that research indicates possible use for photoaging skin, cellulite and striae, and describes the plant as effective in improving treatment of small wounds, hypertrophic wounds, burns, psoriasis and scleroderma [3]. A 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included Centella asiatica among the botanicals compared with peptides, hydroquinone and others, reporting that most cosmeceutical evidence ranged from Level I to Level II, with peptides strongest [7].

Randomised studies published in 2026 tested Centella-containing products. In a 75-person trial in erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, all participants took low-dose oral minocycline for 28 days and used a twice-daily moisturiser; the group using a moisturiser with Centella asiatica, ceramide NP and panthenol showed greater changes in redness measures, facial red area, skin hydration and quality of life than controls [13].

A 12-week blinded multicentre in-use study of a Centella and mandelic acid moisturiser in adults aged 40 to 60 reported lower investigator-rated bruise severity (4.13 to 3.27) with no significant change in days to resolution, and a companion study in crepey skin reported improvements in crepiness, photodamage, firmness, hydration and texture [13]. In a double-blind trial of 112 middle-aged Korean women taking an oral extract for 12 weeks, average wrinkle depth fell 11.1 percent and maximum wrinkle depth 13.3 percent relative to placebo in the per-protocol analysis, with small gains in elasticity and brightness [13]. A review of oral Centella beauty supplements noted design concerns in one wrinkle trial and reported three hepatitis cases [13].

Animal work includes a 2026 study in diabetic rats in which 10 and 20 percent Centella gels changed epithelial thickness, fibroblast counts, collagen and inflammation markers, and a retrospective comparison of two wound-care creams after caesarean section [13].

A 2025 randomised trial in Thailand examined Centella asiatica as an oral supplement in 70 people with type 2 diabetes over six months; after adjustment there were no differences in HbA1c, fasting glucose or LDL cholesterol, and mild gastrointestinal symptoms occurred in 14.7 percent of participants [9][14]. A 2006 randomised trial of Cica-Care silicone gel sheeting, a product unrelated to the herb, enrolled 45 patients with hypertrophic scars and reported reduced scar thickness at 2 and 6 months, with no significant change in pigmentation [8][14]. No clinical study of Centella specifically for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was located.

Topical use can cause contact dermatitis and irritation, and eating it may cause drowsiness. Reviews published in 2024 linked foods and supplements containing the plant to jaundice and liver disease, with case reports of liver disease after several weeks of use [1]. The plant's capacity to absorb pollutants from its environment is noted as a reason raw-material sourcing matters [1]. In the studies above, mild gastrointestinal symptoms and no related serious adverse events were reported [9][13].

Cica is a marketing and ingredient term in the skincare aisle, where it often appears on products aimed at sensitive or acne-prone skin. In supplement and nootropic discussion the herb is called gotu kola. On T Nation, gotu kola is mentioned in threads about supplements for memory, mood and general stacks rather than skin; one poster described using it for memory and said it stabilised their mood, and another forum post lists it as an ingredient in a multi-herb formula [10][11]. A 2025 Hacker News item points to a clinical assessment of scalp health and hair growth with Centella asiatica [12].

lore.intro: Centella is discussed on skincare product pages as a calming ingredient and in supplement threads on T Nation as gotu kola, mostly for memory and mood [10][11].

claims.claim: Cica calms redness and helps skin recover after breakouts
claims.believers: Users and brands describe cica creams and masks as soothing irritated, reddened skin and helping marks fade faster [2][3].
claims.experts: Reviews describe laboratory and animal data on fibroblast activity, collagen synthesis and reduced inflammation in scars; a 2026 randomised trial in rosacea reported greater redness reduction with a Centella-containing moisturiser [2][3][13]. Wikipedia notes clinical efficacy has not been proven in clinical research [1].

claims.believers: Cica is often grouped with brightening and repair products in routines for post-acne marks.
claims.experts: No clinical study of Centella for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was located [1].

claims.claim: Cica treats stretch marks, scars and cellulite
claims.believers: Cosmetic brands and a cosmetology review describe use for striae, cellulite and photoaged skin [3].
claims.experts: The review says research indicates it can be used for these purposes, summarising experimental and clinical work; a 2024 review covers topical wound-healing use [3][5].

claims.claim: Oral gotu kola supplements smooth wrinkles
claims.believers: Beauty supplements and beverages containing the extract are marketed for skin ageing [13].
claims.experts: A 12-week double-blind trial in 112 Korean women reported 11.1 percent lower average wrinkle depth; a critical review noted design concerns in another wrinkle trial and reported three hepatitis cases [13][1].

claims.claim: Gotu kola supplements improve memory and mood
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said experiments with gotu kola for memory had helped stabilise their mood and described an anti-anxiety effect [10].
claims.experts: Reviews describe ethnomedicinal use for memory and brain function [4]; Wikipedia says clinical efficacy and safety are not established and notes drowsiness and liver-related case reports [1].

claims.claim: Natural plant extracts like cica are gentle for everyone
claims.believers: Cica is marketed as a calming option for sensitive skin.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that topical use can cause contact dermatitis and irritation [1].

card.summary: The gotu kola plant behind 'cica' skincare, a traditional soothing herb with no located trials for pigment recovery.
card.aka: Gotu kola, Asiatic pennywort, madecassoside, asiaticoside
card.note: Topical contact dermatitis reported; oral products linked to liver injury case reports.

quick.overview:
Cica is skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, or gotu kola, a herb used traditionally for skin conditions and minor wounds. Its extracts appear in soothing creams and serums.
Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research, and no study on pigment recovery was found.
quick.mechanism: Its main active compounds are triterpenoids such as asiaticoside and madecassoside; no pigment mechanism has been described.
quick.risks: Topical use can cause contact dermatitis or irritation. Oral products have been linked in case reports to liver disease and may cause drowsiness.

chain: Triterpenes soothe irritation and support wound repair
Calmer skin and tidier healing of blemishes and small wounds
Less visible redness and marking, smoother-looking skin
angle.text: People apply cica products to calm redness and support skin as it heals after breakouts or minor injuries, aiming for a more even, less irritated complexion. It is used as a soothing layer in routines alongside moisturisers and sunscreen.
